findings.finding: The author-facing guide src/rebar/_guides/writing-a-passing-plan.md instructs authors to tag [operator-attested] and quotes the coach move 14 template verbatim, but is neither in the CUTOVER nor COMPATIBILITY list — leaving it unclassified and, if left as-is, contradicting the cut-over emit surfaces.
scenarios: After cutover, coach move 14 emits [non-codebase] but the on-ramp guide still teaches authors [operator-attested], contradicting the emit-side surface it is supposed to mirror; the plan's 'accept legacy WITHOUT documenting it' principle does not resolve whether this DOCUMENTED emit surface should cut over.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the completion_verifier.md `kind` emitter: either add the `kind` verdict value (operator-attested → non-codebase) to the CUTOVER (emit) list per ADR 0101 lines 51-53, or state explicitly that the emitted `kind` cutover is owned by another commit and out of scope for S4.
evidence: ADR 0101 lines 51-53: 'The completion-verdict `kind` value changes in lockstep, from operator-attested to non-codebase... Readers accept both values; only the emitter changes.'
completion_verifier.md:224 instructs the LLM to emit `kind`: `codebase-verifiable` or `operator-attested` — an emit surface for the `kind` enum.

Plan CUTOVER (emit) clause names only plan_review_E2/E6/F1.md and coach_moves.py move 14; completion_verifier.md is listed under COMPATIBILITY (recognize both), so the `kind` emitter cutover the ADR mandates is neither scheduled nor stated out-of-scope.
The plan's ACs (emit-side prompts, coach move 14, digests, criteria guide) never mention the emitted `kind` verdict value.
findings.finding: ADR 0101 (the governing decision this plan implements) requires the LLM-emitted completion-verdict `kind` value to cut over 'in lockstep' from `operator-attested` to `non-codebase` ('only the emitter changes'), but the plan places completion_verifier.md solely under COMPATIBILITY (recognize both) and its CUTOVER (emit) list names no `kind`-value emitter — leaving a structured-output enum-emission cutover with ambiguous placement (unscheduled and not explicitly deferred) in this commit.
findings.location: S4 plan — CUTOVER (emit) / COMPATIBILITY lists; completion_verifier.md:224
scenarios: After S4 lands, plans emit `[non-codebase]` tags but the completion verifier still emits `kind: operator-attested`, diverging from the tag the author now writes — the exact divergence ADR 0101 line 52 says the lockstep change exists to prevent.
A reviewer wiring up the audit/page reader (which already accepts both) sees mixed emitted `kind` values across verdicts with no plan direction on which the verifier should now produce.
findings.suggested_fix: Move completion_verifier.md's `kind`-output instruction (completion_verifier.md:224) into the CUTOVER (emit) list so the emitted verdict `kind` becomes `non-codebase` in lockstep with the tag, keeping only its INPUT-tag recognition under COMPATIBILITY; if S4 intends to defer the emitter, say so explicitly and name the owning commit.

findings.finding: Gate 1 (tests/unit/test_measurement_provenance_criterion.py pinning SHA256 digests + line counts) and gate 3 (reviewers/index.json drift gate) are named in 'Why this is ONE commit' as coupled failing gates, but no acceptance criterion names a proving command that these gates pass. findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the What ('accept without documenting it') with AC2 ('recognition-side prompts state the legacy spelling is still accepted') so they agree.
evidence: What: 'teaching the recognition-side surfaces to accept the legacy spelling without documenting it'
AC2: 'Recognition-side prompts state that the legacy spelling is still accepted.'
findings.finding: The What clause says recognition-side surfaces accept the legacy spelling 'WITHOUT documenting it', but AC2 requires recognition-side prompts to 'state that the legacy spelling is still accepted' — these two directions contradict (document it vs. don't).
findings.location: What paragraph vs. Acceptance Criteria line 2
scenarios: Implementer edits recognition prompts to add an explicit 'legacy accepted' note per AC2, then a reviewer flags it as violating the What's 'without documenting it' instruction (or vice versa).
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one policy: if compat must be silent, drop AC2's 'state that...' wording and instead assert the parser/selector recognizes both spellings; if it must be documented, remove 'without documenting it' from the What.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the concrete problem or gap the current `[operator-attested]` spelling causes that motivates cutting over to `[non-codebase]`.
evidence: The 'Why' section states only 'Three gates are coupled to this text and all fail if split' — this motivates atomicity, not the change.
No Expected/Actual, reproduction, or named problem with the current spelling appears anywhere in the plan.
findings.finding: The plan proposes a terminology cutover (emit `[non-codebase]` instead of `[operator-attested]`) but never motivates WHY the spelling must change — the 'Why this is ONE commit' section only justifies the single-commit grouping (coupled gates), not the need for the cutover itself. No named defect, user problem, or gap that the current `[operator-attested]` spelling causes is stated.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a one-line positive rationale (citing ADR-0101 / the 827 live tickets) explaining why emit cuts over while recognition must keep accepting [operator-attested] as an undocumented alias.
evidence: The 'Why this is ONE commit' section justifies commit atomicity (three coupled gates), not the approach itself.
The compatibility rationale (827/4285 live tickets carry [operator-attested]; hard cutover would reclassify them) lives in ADR-0101 but is not referenced in the plan.
G6 checklist item 4: 'The plan states a POSITIVE rationale for the chosen approach (its absence is a finding)'.
findings.finding: The plan states why the change must be ONE commit (gate coupling) but gives no POSITIVE rationale for the chosen emit-cutover/recognize-both APPROACH — why the legacy spelling stays accepted-but-undocumented rather than a hard cutover.
findings.location: 'What' and 'Why this is ONE commit' sections
scenarios: An implementer reading only this plan may not understand why recognition must keep accepting the legacy tag and could 'clean up' the alias, silently reclassifying legacy tickets as codebase-verifiable.
findings.suggested_fix: In 'What', append: 'Recognition keeps accepting [operator-attested] because 827/4285 live tickets carry it (ADR-0101); dropping it would reclassify their attested ACs as codebase-verifiable and break their close path.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the exact legacy string and the exact new `[non-codebase]` literal to be written on emit-side prompts and matched on recognition-side.
evidence: 'Cut the emit-side surfaces over to `[non-codebase]`' — no statement of what exact string this replaces.
Only 'Why' item 1 hints the legacy text is 'OPERATOR-ATTESTED RULE' / '[operator-attested]'.
findings.finding: The literal legacy token and the literal new token are never stated. `[non-codebase]` is used throughout but its exact spelling as it must appear in prompts is unclear, and the 'legacy spelling' is only inferrable indirectly from the _contract_lines selector (`[operator-attested]` / 'OPERATOR-ATTESTED RULE'). The executor must reverse-engineer the source/target strings.
scenarios: Executor writes a slightly different literal (e.g. omits brackets or capitalizes differently), breaking the widened _contract_lines selector match and the recognition prompts.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a line: 'Legacy spelling: `[operator-attested]` / OPERATOR-ATTESTED RULE; new spelling: <exact literal>' so both sides use identical strings.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an acceptance test that a recognition-side surface still matches/accepts the legacy `[operator-attested]` spelling after the cutover (not just the new `[non-codebase]` text).
evidence: Plan: 'teaching the recognition-side surfaces to accept the legacy spelling without documenting it.'
AC pins digests/counts and selector widening but no AC asserts the legacy spelling is still matched by the recognizer.
The cited gates are digest/line-count pins — self-authored-oracle / change-detector style — not behavioral recognition tests.
findings.finding: The COMPATIBILITY requirement — recognition-side prompts must ACCEPT the legacy spelling as well as the new one — introduces a new dual-recognition behavior, but the plan names no test that verifies the legacy spelling is still recognized after cutover. The gates it relies on (SHA256 digest + line-count pins in test_measurement_provenance_criterion.py, validate_criteria_guide, index drift) are byte/structure change-detectors that do not exercise recognition semantics; widening `_contract_lines()` to the new text can pass while legacy recognition silently regresses.
findings.location: COMPATIBILITY (recognize both) list; AC '_contract_lines() selects the new text'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test case feeding the legacy spelling to each recognition-side prompt/selector and asserting it is still recognized (a contract line is found), separate from the digest/count pins.
